stories.title: Brighton Multifamily Draws Record Pool of Potential Buyers
stories.excerpt: Marcus & Millichap closed the sale of 15 Euston Rd., a 24-unit multifamily property in Boston’s Brighton neighborhood. The asset sold for $8,875,000. “Brighton is one of the lowest transactional submarkets in the country for apartment buildings, so it was no surprise that a record number of groups toured this asset,” said Evan Griffith, senior managing director in Marcus & Millichap’s Boston office. Tony Pepdjonovic, senior managing director, added, “The pride of ownership really shines through in this property, and now more than ever, long-term ownership is rewarded by strong operational history and quality product.” Pepdjonovic and Griffith marketed the property on behalf of the seller, a private family. They also procured the buyer, a partnership. 15 Euston Rd. is located in Brighton, 0.1 miles from Sutherland Road Station. The 19,200-square-foot property sits on a 0.22-acre lot with off-street parking. It was built in 1962 and has four stories. The post Brighton Multifamily Draws Record Pool of Potential Buyers appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Marcus & Millichap sold 24-unit Brighton property at 15 Euston Rd., Boston for $8.875M.
Record buyer interest in low-transaction Brighton submarket signals pent-up demand for small multifamily.
Property near transit (Sutherland Station) with strong operations attracted multiple offers despite small size.
stories.summary: Marcus & Millichap closed the sale of a 24-unit multifamily property at 15 Euston Rd. in Boston's Brighton neighborhood for $8.875 million, drawing a record number of potential buyers. The 1962-built, 19,200-square-foot asset sits 0.1 miles from transit and offered off-street parking. The brokerage noted Brighton is one of the lowest-transaction multifamily submarkets in the country, making the robust bid process notable.
stories.impact: Brighton's thinness as a transaction market—paired with record buyer interest—signals investors view small multifamily near Boston transit as underpriced relative to demand. Developers should evaluate whether Brighton or similar transit-proximate submarkets in mature markets are ripe for small-scale new construction or adaptive reuse to capture value from supply-constrained neighborhoods.

stories.title: CP Group Sells Third Boca Raton Office for $79M
stories.excerpt: CP Group has sold off yet another office complex in Boca Raton, Fla. The office investor, alongside Chicago-based Harrison Street Asset Management, sold One Boca Place for $78.9 million, property records show. Golden East Investors purchased the 286,890-square-foot asset at 2255 Glades Road, located just west of Interstate 95, near the Town Center at Boca Raton indoor mall. The two-building office property was constructed in 1986 on a 7.6-acre parcel. City National Bank of Florida provided an $82.1 million loan to the New York-based buyer. The sale produced little appreciation for the sellers, who bought the complex for $76.4 million in 2014. The transaction marks the third office property since the summer that CP Group has sold in Boca Raton, where it is headquartered. In September, the firm sold the Two Town Center property for $62 million to Joe Sitt’s Thor Equities. This summer, it also offloaded the 124-acre, 1.7-million-square-foot BRiC campus for an undisclosed amount to Stephen Ross’s Related Ross. Representatives for CP Group and Golden East Investors did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Julia Echikson can be reached at jechikson@commercialobserserv.com.
bullets: CP Group, Harrison Street sold One Boca Place office complex for $78.9M; minimal appreciation since 2014 purchase.
Third Boca Raton office sale by CP Group since summer; flagship HQ market seeing recurring dispositions.
Golden East Investors acquired 286,890 SF property with $82.1M financing; lender signaling capital availability despite flat returns.
stories.summary: CP Group and Harrison Street Asset Management sold One Boca Place, a 286,890-square-foot, two-building office complex in Boca Raton, Florida, for $78.9 million to Golden East Investors. The 1986-built asset on 7.6 acres produced negligible appreciation for the sellers, who purchased it for $76.4 million in 2014. This marks CP Group's third Boca Raton office disposal since summer, with City National Bank providing $82.1 million in financing.
stories.impact: CP Group's repeated office exits from its own headquarters market suggest accelerating shift away from legacy office holdings despite senior management presence. The minimal gain on a 10-year hold and ready bank financing indicate institutional capital remains available for office acquisitions, but seller conviction is eroding—a signal that Boca Raton office fundamentals are challenged and multifamily may offer better risk-adjusted returns in that market.

stories.title: New York City’s Pied-à-Terre Surcharge Changes the Investment Calculation
stories.excerpt: Whether you’re selling a walk-up with a restaurant downstairs, a rental building or a luxury apartment, new rules can change what a property is worth and who will buy it. That’s why New York City’s pied-à-terre surcharge belongs in the investment conversation. The tax doesn’t apply to all these properties, but the differences in how they are treated matter when buyers compare their options. The measure was heralded as a levy on absentee billionaires, projected to bring in around $500 million in new annual revenue for the city. Mayor Zohran Mamdani called it a tax when he announced its rollout over the summer. The law calls it a surcharge. Trystan Polsinelli. PHOTO: Courtesy Compass The legal distinction matters. Ongoing lawsuits challenge whether its revenue can be excluded from the city’s constitutional real estate tax limit. Separate litigation has challenged how the city identified properties potentially subject to the charge. The courts will decide those issues. In the meantime, buyers and sellers have deals to negotiate. Who owned the property, who lived there, and whether it was held through a trust or an LLC are all questions that can affect whether the charge applies, what the property costs to own, and what a buyer is willing to pay. Whatever the name, the surcharge is an additional annual expense for properties where it applies. For the 2026–27 and 2027–28 tax years, affected residential condos and co-ops face rates of 4 percent to 6.5 percent of the applicable Department of Finance value. That’s the city’s valuation, not necessarily the purchase price. Some second-home owners also stand to lose a co-op or condo tax abatement they’ll no longer qualify for. Co-op owners face a particular concern. A charge associated with one apartment is billed through the co-op corporation, rather than billed directly to that unit’s shareholder. bullets: NYC pied-à-terre surcharge (est. $500M annual revenue) applies to ~2,100 properties; legal challenges ongoing.
Tax treatment differs by ownership structure (trust, LLC), complicating investment underwriting and buyer qualification.
Surcharge changes valuation math for rental buildings, walk-ups, and luxury apartments; impacts buyer pool and prices.
stories.summary: New York City's new pied-à-terre surcharge—projected to generate $500 million in annual revenue—has created uncertainty in the residential investment market as buyers and sellers negotiate deals. The tax's legal definition as a 'surcharge' (not a tax) is being challenged in court; ownership structure, prior occupancy, and entity type determine applicability, creating complexity in underwriting. Multiple lawsuits question revenue treatment and property identification methodology.
stories.impact: The pied-à-terre surcharge introduces deal-level underwriting friction and valuation uncertainty across Manhattan residential assets, particularly small multifamily and rental buildings. Developers acquiring or financing rental properties in NYC must now model surcharge liability and potential future legal changes into acquisition underwriting, and may face tighter loan terms from lenders uncomfortable with regulatory tail risk—potentially delaying or reducing starts in Manhattan through 2026 until courts clarify liability.

stories.title: Investor Acquires Lowe’s Ground Lease in Kent
stories.excerpt: Northmarq closed the sale of a 10.62-acre Lowe’s ground lease located at 24050 Pacific Hwy S. in Kent, Washington. Northmarq represented the seller, with the firm’s Pacific Northwest Investment Sales team, led by Sean Tufts, Kevin Adatto, Joe Dugoni, and Jack Hallberg, brokering the deal in collaboration with Austin Cohn of Wahl & Associates. The buyer was a private East Coast-based group, as part of a 1031 exchange. “Our team ran a competitive process, securing multiple offers before moving forward with the group that recognized both the investment-grade tenancy and long-term upside of the low-rent ground lease,” Tufts said. “This transaction also continues the trend of out-of-market capital gravitating towards the Pacific Northwest, where new retail development is nearly impossible to pencil.” Built in 2006, the 135,041-square-foot store sits on 10.62 acres, one block south of the Kent Des Moines Link light rail station, which opened in December 2025 as part of the Federal Way Link Extension. The post Investor Acquires Lowe’s Ground Lease in Kent appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Northmarq sold 10.62-acre Lowe's ground lease in Kent, WA to East Coast investor via 1031 exchange.
Property sits one block from Kent Des Moines Link light rail, opened December 2025 (Federal Way Extension).
Out-of-market capital gravitating to Pacific Northwest retail given new retail development is 'nearly impossible to pencil.'
stories.summary: Northmarq brokered the sale of a 10.62-acre Lowe's ground lease at 24050 Pacific Hwy S. in Kent, Washington, to an East Coast-based investor as part of a 1031 exchange. The 135,041-square-foot store, built in 2006, is located one block south of the Kent Des Moines Link light rail station, which opened in December 2025 as part of the Federal Way Link Extension. The transaction highlights investor appetite for transit-proximate retail in the Pacific Northwest.
stories.impact: New light rail connectivity to Kent (Federal Way Link, Dec 2025 opening) is attracting institutional capital seeking ground-lease stability in a market where new retail development is structurally constrained. Multifamily developers should monitor similar transit completions in Seattle-Tacoma and Portland markets; rail opens land around stations for mixed-use/residential redevelopment, and investor competition for existing retail may compress retail cap rates, improving feasibility for multifamily-centric mixed-use projects near stations.

stories.title: NY City Council Passes Bill Giving Nonprofits First Dibs on Distressed Apartment Properties
stories.excerpt: The New York City Council on Thursday passed the Community Option to Purchase Act (COPA), which gives nonprofit groups a 90-day window to potentially acquire distressed apartment buildings after they’re put up for sale. The measure now goes to Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who has signaled his approval in recent months. An earlier version of the bill was vetoed by then-Mayor Eric Adams last year. Industry groups including the Real Estate Board of New York were opposed to the previous version, which covered more than 10,000 apartment buildings. The bill as enacted Thursday covers an estimated 2,100, according to the city’s Department of Housing Preservation and Development. “REBNY appreciates the constructive engagement and thoughtful leadership of Speaker [Julie] Menin and Council Member [Sandy] Nurse, which has resulted in a more targeted and practical bill,” REBNY President James Whelan told the New York Post. Nurse introduced a revised COPA earlier this year. The post NY City Council Passes Bill Giving Nonprofits First Dibs on Distressed Apartment Properties appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: NYC Council passed COPA; gives nonprofits 90-day right of first refusal on ~2,100 distressed apartment buildings.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani expected to sign; REBNY initially opposed but accepted narrowed scope (2,100 vs. 10,000 units).
Bill applies to distressed properties sold after passage; creates timeline friction for for-profit acquisitions and dispositions.
stories.summary: The New York City Council passed the Community Option to Purchase Act (COPA), granting nonprofit organizations a 90-day window to acquire distressed apartment buildings before for-profit buyers can close. The measure, now heading to Mayor Zohran Mamdani for expected approval, covers approximately 2,100 buildings—a narrower scope than an earlier version opposed by the Real Estate Board of New York. An earlier iteration was vetoed by then-Mayor Eric Adams.
stories.impact: COPA injects a 90-day delay into for-profit multifamily acquisition timelines across ~2,100 NYC buildings deemed 'distressed' and introduces competition from nonprofits with different return thresholds and financing (often tax-exempt bonds). For-profit developers and investors should assume extended hold-and-operate periods on acquisitions, higher carry costs, and lower acquisition prices to account for nonprofit optionality—effectively narrowing the pool of distressed assets available to commercial developers and potentially reducing price discovery in NYC's secondary/tertiary multifamily market.

stories.title: Marcus & Millichap Capital Corporation Arranges $25M Financing for Michigan Retail Property
stories.excerpt: Marcus & Millichap Capital Corporation (MMCC) announced that Todd Phillips, managing director in MMCC’s Raleigh office, secured $25 million in financing for the acquisition of a 62,364-square-foot retail property located at 700 West Big Beaver Road in Troy, Michigan. The loan was secured with a national bank and features a seven-year term, a 6.125% interest rate and a 30-year amortization period. The property is occupied by several national restaurants and retailers. It is situated in a highly trafficked area near Interstate 75, providing strong visibility and convenient regional access. “This financing reflects the strength of the property’s location and tenant mix,” said Phillips. “We were pleased to secure attractive, long-term financing that supports our client’s acquisition objectives.” The property is located within the City Center office complex, a 13-story, 297,530-square-foot mixed-use tower that has undergone extensive renovations and is approximately 95% percent occupied. The post Marcus & Millichap Capital Corporation Arranges $25M Financing for Michigan Retail Property appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Marcus & Millichap arranged $25M financing for 62,364 SF retail acquisition in Troy, Michigan at 6.125% rate.
Seven-year term, 30-year amortization; property near I-75 with national restaurant/retail tenants in mixed-use complex.
Retail financing at sub-6.5% reflects strong national tenant credit and location quality; capital availability for core retail.
stories.summary: Marcus & Millichap Capital Corporation secured $25 million in financing for a 62,364-square-foot retail property acquisition at 700 West Big Beaver Road in Troy, Michigan. The loan features a seven-year term, 6.125% interest rate, and 30-year amortization, provided by a national bank. The property is occupied by national restaurant and retail tenants and is part of the City Center office complex, which is 95% occupied.
stories.impact: Sub-6.5% retail financing for stabilized, national-tenant properties signals lenders are comfortable with retail credit quality and urban location—but this is exceptions-based pricing for trophy assets. For multifamily developers, the takeaway is that lender appetite for retail-heavy mixed-use is intact when anchored by credit tenants; however, rising Treasury yields (noted in Article 9) may be lifting floors on new originations, so locking construction financing windows is critical.

stories.title: Revamp NYC Wants to Bring 99 Units to the Financial District’s 160 Pearl Street
stories.excerpt: Manhattan’s Financial District was once known only for offices and workers, with its liveliness ending at the close of happy hour. But over the last several years, the neighborhood has transformed into a hub of residential communities. The latest residential project getting added to the mix might be a 99-unit rental. Revamp NYC, a New York-based residential development and property construction firm, has filed an application with the New York City Department of Buildings (DOB) for a new housing development at 160 Pearl Street. If approved, the proposed mixed-use building would stand 25 stories and include 99 units, as well as amenities such as indoor and outdoor recreation space, a yoga room, and 2,394 square feet of ground-floor retail space. Revamp’s Israel Tishler submitted the plans and is listed as the property owner on the DOB application, while Navkiran Cheema of KMA Designs is named as the architect and applicant. Revamp and KMA Designs did not immediately respond to Commercial Observer’s requests for comment. It is unclear if Revamp intends to make 160 Pearl Street an affordable housing property. Under New York’s 485-x tax incentive, buildings with 99 or fewer units can get a significant tax break when building affordable housing, while not being subject to certain construction worker wage requirements that are mandatory in larger projects of 100 units or more. It’s also unclear whether Revamp plans to demolish the existing six-story commercial building at 160 Pearl Street, which is home to financial consultancy firms Ikahn Capital and Hybrid Funder, as well as Irish pub The Full Shilling in the ground-floor retail space. Amanda Schiavo can be reached at aschiavo@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Revamp NYC filed 25-story, 99-unit residential project at 160 Pearl Street, Financial District, Manhattan.
Project includes 2,394 SF ground-floor retail, recreation/yoga amenities; unclear if pursuing 485-x affordable housing tax abatement.
Financial District residential pipeline growing as office-to-residential conversion accelerates in lower Manhattan.
stories.summary: Revamp NYC filed a Department of Buildings application for a 25-story, 99-unit mixed-use residential development at 160 Pearl Street in Manhattan's Financial District. The proposed building includes 2,394 square feet of ground-floor retail and amenities such as indoor/outdoor recreation and a yoga room. Affordable housing status remains unclear, and Revamp did not respond to requests for comment.
stories.impact: Financial District continues conversion from office-centric to residential-mixed-use; 99 units signals market confidence in lower Manhattan residential demand and feasible economics despite redevelopment costs and retail challenges. Multifamily developers entering Financial District should expect competitive pressure from conversion specialists like Revamp; ground-floor retail remains difficult to lease despite amenities, suggesting retail as a capital sink rather than revenue engine—model accordingly on future FiDi residential acquisitions.

stories.title: Skanska Signs Lease at 17xM to Bring DC Office Building to 93% Leased
stories.excerpt: Skanska announced a new lease with Café Unido at 17xM, filling the final portion of the building’s 13,500 square feet of ground-floor retail in downtown Washington, D.C. The milestone comes as 17xM’s office space reaches 93% leased overall. Located at 1700 M Street NW in the city’s central business district, 17xM continues to attract tenants seeking a combination of workspace, amenities and a mix of retail and dining options. “Today’s tenants are making long-term decisions about how their workplaces support collaboration, culture and employee experience,” said Mark Carroll, executive vice president at Skanska USA Commercial Development. “17xM’s leasing momentum reflects a broader shift toward office environments that are adaptable, hospitality-driven and designed to remain competitive over time.” Café Unido will join Uchi, a Japanese restaurant concept, which is now open at 17xM. Designed by Kohn Pedersen Fox Associates, 17xM is an 11-story trophy office tower. Leasing for the property is being overseen by CBRE’s Randy Harrell, Joe Coleman and Lara Nealon. The post Skanska Signs Lease at 17xM to Bring DC Office Building to 93% Leased appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Skanska's 17xM office tower in Washington DC reached 93% leased; final ground-floor retail (Café Unido) filled.
11-story trophy office by KPF with hospitality-driven design; emphasizes employee experience and collaboration culture.
Strong retail/amenity leasing despite tight office market reflects tenant demand for experiential workplace environments.
stories.summary: Skanska announced a lease with Café Unido at 17xM, filling the final 13,500 square feet of ground-floor retail at the downtown Washington, D.C. office tower. The 11-story trophy office, designed by Kohn Pedersen Fox, has reached 93% occupancy overall. The project combines workspace, amenities, and retail/dining to attract tenants prioritizing collaboration, culture, and employee experience.
stories.impact: 17xM's 93% leasing despite Washington DC's soft office market indicates trophy trophy office with strong hospitality programming and amenities can outperform; however, this is an elite asset in a top submarket. For multifamily developers, the signal is that mixed-use office-retail-dining combinations are viable if anchored by class-A office and premium tenants—but conversions of secondary office stock to residential may be more attractive than trying to stabilize legacy office.

stories.title: Rexford Sells $1.3B in SoCal Industrial Assets as Leasing Rebounds
stories.excerpt: Rexford Industrial Realty continued its transformation from Southern California’s biggest industrial buyer into one of its largest sellers during the third quarter after completing $1.3 billion in property sales. The Los Angeles-based real estate investment trust (REIT) sold 25 properties totaling 5.5 million square feet during the quarter, including the previously announced $1.2 billion sale to EQT Real Estate. Rexford has now sold $1.5 billion in properties this year as part of its $2 billion portfolio realignment strategy. CEO Laura Clark said during the REIT’s third-quarter earnings call Friday that the company expects to complete most of the remaining $500 million in planned sales by the end of this year, although rising Treasury yields could complicate deals. “While recent increases in Treasury rates are impacting the cost of capital for certain buyers, and bringing more selectivity to the transaction market, engagement around the remaining disposition assets remains constructive,” Clark said. The EQT portfolio sale, Rexford’s largest deal ever, had a weighted average remaining lease term of just 2.7 years with rents nearly 30 percent above market rates, according to Chief Operating Officer John Nahas. The company also sold three properties totaling approximately 251,000 square feet to owner-users for $86 million. Conversely, Rexford made no acquisitions during the third quarter. Clark said acquisitions remain part of Rexford’s long-term strategy, but not at the expense of other investments. “Today, other uses of capital are more compelling,” she said. “We can afford to be patient. … Our portfolio realignment objective was about owning the right real estate and the right markets.” Meanwhile, Rexford recorded 116 leases covering 3.74 million square feet during the third quarter, up from 2.1 million square feet the previous quarter, and up from the 3.27 million square feet in the same quarter last year. bullets: Rexford Industrial sold $1.3B in SoCal industrial (25 properties, 5.5M SF) in Q3; $1.5B YTD out of $2B plan.
Rising Treasury yields creating headwinds for remaining $500M in planned dispositions; buyer selectivity increasing.
CEO notes engagement 'constructive' but capital cost pressures evident; leasing rebound supporting fundamentals.
stories.summary: Rexford Industrial completed $1.3 billion in Southern California industrial asset sales during Q3, selling 25 properties totaling 5.5 million square feet, including a $1.2 billion portfolio to EQT Real Estate. Year-to-date, Rexford has sold $1.5 billion of its targeted $2 billion portfolio realignment strategy. CEO Laura Clark warned that rising Treasury yields are increasing buyer selectivity and complicating the remaining $500 million in planned dispositions.
stories.impact: Rexford's aggressive disposition (REIT shifting from buyer to seller role) signals peak SoCal industrial values; rising Treasury yields and buyer selectivity are now real friction points in execution. Multifamily developers should track Rexford's remaining dispositions and buyer composition—if trophy industrial off-market, it suggests capital is rotating out of real estate entirely (into Treasuries) rather than redeploying into multifamily, pressuring equity availability and cap rates across SoCal.

stories.title: Roof of Concept: Meet Jeff Thramann, a Data Center Disruptor
stories.excerpt: Jeff Thramann has always been an outside-the-box thinker. A trained neurosurgeon with a degree from Cornell Medical School, Thramann is an entrepreneur at heart and an inventor by nature. He’s been issued north of 130 patents and has seen his inventive startups like U.S. Radiosurgery sold to a publicly traded company and Denver CyberKnife (another cancer treatment facility) bought by a private firm. But it was in the renewable energy space — particularly his interest in creating technology that mitigates the effects of air pollution — where Thramann found his current calling, one that has indirectly pushed him into the data center space, where he and a well-known former politician are creating a new innovation that may disrupt the entire data center industry. Today, Thramann is the CEO of LT350, a data center infrastructure company he formed last year with former U.S. Secretary of Defense Mark Esper, which aims to install mini data centers on the roofs of solar power canopies above the open-air parking lots of properties such as malls, hospitals or schools. The thinking is this: By integrating solar panels with small modular cartridges that consist of graphics processing units (GPU), battery storage and inverters, the tech-fitted roof will essentially turn the airspace above any parking lot into a data center for low latency inference. How Thramann got to this new business plan is a story in itself. After investing into solar panels and the uses of battery-powered technology 20 years ago, Thramann was drawn to electric cars through an association made with Kimle Musk (Elon’s brother) in Boulder, Colo. (Fun fact: Thramann purchased Tesla car No. 541 off the assembly line back in 2008.) bullets: Jeff Thramann (former neurosurgeon, 130+ patents) founded LT350 with Mark Esper to install mini data centers on parking-lot solar canopies.
Technology aims to integrate solar + modular data center infrastructure on retail/hospital/school parking lots.
Emerging data center model targets alternative real estate (non-purpose-built) and renewable energy co-location; disruptive to traditional data center development.
stories.summary: Jeff Thramann, a trained neurosurgeon with 130+ patents, founded LT350 with former U.S. Secretary of Defense Mark Esper to disrupt the data center industry. The company installs small modular data centers on solar power canopies above open-air parking lots at retail, hospital, and school properties. LT350 is pursuing a distributed, renewable-energy-integrated data center model that diverges from traditional purpose-built facilities.
stories.impact: LT350's rooftop data center model on existing retail/institutional parking is largely tangential to multifamily development but signals emerging competition for rooftop/outdoor space and renewable energy infrastructure. Multifamily developers in markets with strong solar/tech demand (Austin, Phoenix, Denver, Seattle) should monitor whether data center use-rights or solar canopies become tenant/operator negotiation points; if LT350 scales, it could reduce available rooftop space for multifamily amenities or solar-for-revenue models, or create co-tenancy issues on mixed-use projects.
